Glossary

HTTPS and SSL certificate: what is that little padlock?

HTTPS is the protected version of a website address: whatever travels between the visitor and you is scrambled for prying eyes. The SSL certificate is the piece that makes this protection possible.

The definition in one sentence

When an address starts with https:// and a padlock appears next to it, the information sent is encrypted. Nobody can read it on the way, even on station wifi.

The SSL certificate (also called TLS, its newer name) is a kind of ID card for the website. It proves to the browser that the site really is who it claims to be, and it is used to encrypt the exchanges.

What it does for a small business

You may think your website does not send anything secret. Yet as soon as a customer fills in your form, they send their name, their phone number, sometimes their address. That data deserves to be protected.

HTTPS also brings:

  • Trust. Without it, browsers show “Not secure” next to your address. Many visitors leave straight away.
  • A warmer welcome from Google. The search engine prefers protected websites.
  • The right to sell. No serious payment method accepts a website without HTTPS.

A real-life example

A dressmaker opens her website on her phone to show a customer. At the top of the screen: “Not secure”. The customer asks if it is dangerous. Nothing serious was wrong with the site, but the question was enough to sow doubt. A certificate would have settled the matter.

What you need to know

  • A certificate expires. It must be renewed regularly. If it is forgotten, the browser shows a red warning page that scares everyone away.
  • The padlock does not mean the site is honest. It only means the connection is protected. A dubious site can have one too.
  • The whole website must use HTTPS, not just the form page. A single image loaded without protection can make the padlock disappear.

If your website still shows “Not secure” today, that is the first thing to fix, even before the design.

Your questions

Do you have to pay for an SSL certificate?

There are free certificates, recognised by every browser, that suit a business website very well. Paid certificates are mainly for very large organisations. What matters is that it is installed correctly and renewed on time.

How can I tell if my website uses HTTPS?

Open it and look at the address bar. A padlock or a settings icon to the left of the address means all is well. The words “Not secure” mean the certificate is missing.
